rows.comparison: Trade data cannot help here. The catalogue has no capacity figures for Bangladesh.
rows.balance_note: Not built yet. Bangladesh does not report its trade to UN Comtrade, and no figure for its smelters' output was found. Wilson's 2020 inventory for UNEP put used batteries at about 118,000 t a year (about 71 kt of lead), three-quarters of it from 1.5 million e-rickshaws whose batteries last about six months. Battery-run rickshaws and easy-bikes are now put at 4.5 to 6 million (BPDB, CPD, 2026) or over 6 million (BRTA, 2025); scaling Wilson's e-rickshaw line to those numbers gives roughly 300,000–390,000 t of used batteries a year, or about 180–230 kt of lead, a rough figure only.

rows.production_note: Secondary refined lead, 2022, a USGS estimate.
rows.production_source: USGS Minerals Yearbook 2022, lead, table 14 (reproduced by IndexMundi)
rows.trade_note: Reported by Indonesia; no lead scrap trade recorded.
rows.comparison: Exports rose from about 21 kt (2023) to 39 kt (2024). Catalogued capacity is now about 119 kt of lead, mostly figures from Wilson's 2021 inventory, but all five catalogued plants are graded stale (D). USGS estimates 55 kt (2022). The rise points to active smelters not yet confirmed.
rows.balance_method: Provisional: lead in Indonesia's own used batteries is Wilson's 2021 estimate from batteries in use, and smelter feed is secondary lead output ÷ recovery.
balance_notes: Lead in Indonesia's own used batteries comes from Wilson's 2021 inventory for Pure Earth: about 403,000 t of used batteries a year from about 925,000 t in use (vehicle and battery counts from around 2020), with car and motorcycle batteries lasting two years and commercial ones three. The low case gives them three and four years (about 275,000 t). The counts are dated, so the figure is approximate for 2024.

Industrial smelter output is USGS's estimate of 55 kt of secondary lead (2022) in the central case. Refined lead exports (38.6 kt in 2024) are the low case, a floor, since Indonesia's battery makers also use recycled lead; the high case is the formal licensed sector's 106,000 t of capacity in Wilson's inventory, run full.
Used-battery and scrap trade is small: Indonesia recorded 104 t of used-battery exports in 2024 and no lead scrap trade.

Wilson's inventory reaches the same conclusion: the formal sector, even running full, recycles less than half the lead in Indonesia's used batteries, and over 130,000 t of lead bullion a year may come from informal smelters.
Indonesia also exported 40.6 kt of new lead-acid batteries in 2024, and about 390,000 vehicles a year with batteries fitted (Wilson); those batteries are scrapped abroad and are not in the estimate.

rows.production_note: Secondary refined lead, 2022, a USGS estimate.
rows.production_source: USGS Minerals Yearbook 2022, lead, table 14 (reproduced by IndexMundi)
rows.trade_note: Reported by Nigeria; UN Comtrade estimated the weight of refined lead exports. No lead scrap exports recorded. Used-battery trade is what partners recorded; Nigeria recorded none.
rows.comparison: Exports of 39–44 kt a year (2023–2024) are about three times the only catalogued capacity figure (Ibeto, NG-008) and match USGS's 36 kt estimate: Nigeria has active smelters that the catalogue does not yet capture, or lacks their capacity figures.
rows.balance_method: Smelter output is measured by refined lead exports, as for Ghana.
balance_notes: Lead in Nigeria's own used batteries is the lead in new lead-acid batteries it imported in 2020–2022, less those it exported. Nigeria reported exporting 8.2 kt of batteries in 2022, 7.3 kt of them to Ghana, which recorded 9 t from Nigeria; leaving those exports out would add about 1.6 kt of lead to the central figure.

Smelter intake is refined lead exports divided by recovery, which assumes Nigeria uses little refined lead at home. The exports, 39.0 kt, are close to USGS's estimate of 36 kt of secondary lead produced in 2022.
Used-battery trade is what partners recorded (52 t from Niger, 98 t to India); Nigeria recorded none.

Recorded supply covers 23% of what the smelters take in. Possible sources of the rest: batteries in imported used vehicles, batteries brought in without being declared, and used batteries carried across land borders. One catalogued plant belongs to a battery maker (Ibeto Group); batteries made in Nigeria would add lead that the trade figures miss.
Informal breakers who sell lead to exporting smelters end up inside the export figure, so the national balance cannot see informal work upstream of the smelters.

rows.production_source: USGS Minerals Yearbook 2022, lead, table 14 (reproduced by IndexMundi)
rows.trade_note: Reported by DR Congo; no refined lead exports or lead scrap trade recorded in 2024. Used-battery exports add the shipments only partners recorded (4.8 kt, mostly in Rwanda’s imports).
rows.comparison: DR Congo recorded 1.2 kt of refined lead exports in 2023 and none in 2024. Its one catalogued smelter, Anodos in Lubumbashi (CD-001), casts lead into anodes for the copper and cobalt industry; its company profile gives 5,000 t a year of lead billets. Used-battery exports in 2024: 1.9 kt recorded by DR Congo (to Mauritius and the UAE) and 4.8 kt recorded only by partners, mostly Rwanda.
rows.balance_method: Its one smelter's lead stays in the country, so the balance turns on used batteries exported.
balance_notes: Lead in DR Congo's own used batteries is the lead in new lead-acid batteries it imported in 2020–2022, less those it exported.
Used batteries exported are DR Congo's own record (1.9 kt, to Mauritius and the UAE) plus shipments only its partners recorded (4.8 kt: Rwanda 4.1 kt, India 0.6 kt).

DR Congo recorded no refined lead exports in 2024, so nothing is counted as fed to smelters. Its one catalogued smelter, in Lubumbashi, casts lead into anodes for the copper and cobalt industry; counting what it makes would widen the gap.

More lead leaves in used batteries than DR Congo's recorded battery imports supply. That points to batteries arriving unrecorded (in imported used vehicles or across land borders) or to used batteries from neighbouring countries passing through.
In 2023 partners recorded 6.4 kt of used batteries from DR Congo, mostly in Rwanda; DR Congo recorded none.

rows.production_source: USGS Minerals Yearbook 2022, lead, table 14 (reproduced by IndexMundi)
rows.trade_note: Reported by Ethiopia for 2023; it has not reported 2024. Its export weights for used batteries, scrap and refined lead are high for their declared values; UNCTAD puts the used-battery exports at 1.0 kt rather than 4.0 kt.
rows.comparison: Little lead is exported (0.3 kt in 2023), while Ethiopia exported 3–4 kt of ULABs a year in 2022–2023 (in 2023, all to India), consistent with no active smelter in the catalogue.
rows.balance_method: No industrial smelter is active; the balance counts what left the country in used batteries, scrap and refined lead.
balance_notes: Lead in Ethiopia's own used batteries is the lead in new lead-acid batteries it imported in 2019–2021. The balance assumes no battery making at home: the Awash battery factory, which also recycled batteries, stopped about a decade ago.

Used batteries exported are UNCTAD's estimate of 1.0 kt, all to India, which recorded the same. Ethiopia itself reported 4.0 kt, a weight UNCTAD treats as implausible for the value; counting that instead would leave 85% unaccounted.

Refined lead exports (328 t) are counted as smelter output and scrap exports (580 t) as leaving the country, although both were declared at low values for their weight and no industrial smelter is active in the catalogue.

The unaccounted lead is in used batteries that were neither exported nor smelted industrially: broken and smelted informally, or still stockpiled or dumped. Batteries fitted to imported used vehicles are not counted and would add to it.

rows.trade_note: Reported by Argentina: refined lead exports and battery trade. Refined lead imports and lead scrap trade are not yet checked. Argentina recorded no used-battery imports or exports in 2023 or 2024.
rows.comparison: Exports are small (0.5 kt in 2023, 1.5 kt in 2024) and Argentina reported no ULAB imports or exports, so its recycled lead stays in the country, as Wilson's 2021 inventory also found. USGS's 85 kt estimate of secondary output (2022) is above the catalogued plants' lead capacity (about 68 kt, all graded D), so capacity figures or plants are missing.
rows.balance_note: Not built yet: refined lead imports and lead scrap trade are not yet checked. Wilson's 2021 inventory put Argentina's used batteries at about 155,000 t a year (about 93 kt of lead), close to USGS's estimate of 85 kt of secondary lead output (2022); with no used-battery exports and no sign of informal recycling, Wilson concluded that domestic smelters recycle nearly all of them.
